hook: See what's powering your area right now, from just your postcode.
slides: Type in your postcode and we'll show you what's powering your area right now.
You'll see the power stations it's likely coming from, and where your gas started out.
And the cleanest time to run the washing or charge the car.
It's an estimate from public data, because electricity all mixes on the grid. Nobody can trace it exactly.
closing: It's free, with no account needed. Link in bio. Where's yours from?
caption:
Every time you boil the kettle, the power came from somewhere. A wind farm off the coast, a gas plant down the road, a cable under the sea from another country. Most of us never get to see that.

So we built a free site that shows you. Type in your postcode and you'll see what's powering your area right now, where your gas started out, and the cleanest time to put the washing on.

We'll be posting here most days: what's happening on the grid, how far things have come, what's just been built, and how all of this works. Each kind of post has its own colour, so you can find the ones you like.

What would you most like to know about where your energy comes from?

hook: Nobody can trace which power station boils your kettle. Here's how we work it out anyway.
slides: Electricity all mixes together once it's on the grid. There's no way to follow it to one home.
So we make an informed estimate, using public data on what's running right now.
We match those power stations to the real high-voltage lines near you.
Then each fuel's share is split between its stations. Bigger and closer ones count for more.
closing: It's the most likely answer, not a certainty. Want to see yours?
caption:
Here's a slightly awkward truth about electricity: once it's on the grid, it's all mixed together. Nobody can trace the power in your socket back to one place.

What we can do is work out what's most likely, using live public data and the real map of high-voltage lines.

Which power station would you guess is feeding your home right now?

hook: Your gas came into Britain somewhere. Here's how we work out where.
slides: National Gas publishes how much gas is entering Britain at each terminal.
We give every terminal a share based on how much is flowing, and how far away it is from you.
Gas landing through the Langeled pipeline at Easington counts as Norwegian.
Gas at Milford Haven and the Isle of Grain arrived on tankers.
closing: Gas mixes in the pipes too, so it's a best estimate. Curious where yours started out?
caption:
Gas doesn't come with a label on it. It all mixes in the pipes on its way to your boiler.

But Britain's entry points are public, so we can work out where the gas near you most likely started, whether that's a North Sea field, Norway or a tanker from across the ocean.

Where do you think yours came from today?

hook: There's a cleanest time to put your washing on. Here's how we find it.
slides: We read the carbon forecast for your region, up to 24 hours ahead.
Then we hunt for the cleanest stretch that actually suits real life.
A wash is treated as a 2.5 hour cycle, between 07:00 and 22:00. Nobody wants a 3am spin.
A car gets a 6 hour charge, between 19:00 and 07:00.
closing: Same wash, different hour, different carbon. When's your best time today?
caption:
The cleanest hour of the day is no use if it's 3am and you're asleep.

So when we pick your best time, we only look at hours when you'd realistically press the button: daytime and evening for washing, overnight for the car.

What's the one job you'd happily move to a cleaner time?

hook: 'Renewable' can mean different things. Here's exactly what we count.
slides: We count four things: wind, solar, hydro and biomass.
Biomass is included because that's how the official figures treat it, and we always say so.
Gas and coal count as fossil fuels. Nuclear and imports are shown on their own.
Britain is split into 14 regions, so your figure is for your whole region.
closing: Now you know how we count. How renewable is your region right now?
caption:
Percentages only mean something if you know what's being counted.

So here's exactly what goes into our renewable figure, and what doesn't. We'd rather you knew than took our word for it.

Does anything on that list surprise you?

hook: Your full address stays on your device. Here's what happens when you type it in.
slides: Your full address and postcode stay in your browser.
Only the first half of your postcode, like SW9, ever leaves your device.
That's enough to fetch your region's forecast and place you on the map.
Your location on the map is the middle of your postcode district, not your home.
closing: No accounts. No tracking cookies. Just where your energy comes from.
caption:
A site that asks for your address should be able to say exactly what it does with it.

The short version: it stays on your device. We only ever use the first half of your postcode.

Is there anything else you'd like us to explain about how this works?

hook: Every figure on our site comes from free, public data. Here's whose.
slides: The forecast comes from the Carbon Intensity API, run by NESO with the University of Oxford and partners.
Which stations are running comes from Elexon's public data.
Gas flows come from National Gas, and renewable sites from a government database.
Power lines and pipeline routes are mapped by OpenStreetMap contributors.
closing: All public. All free for anyone to check. We just put it in one place for you.
caption:
None of this is secret. Britain publishes a remarkable amount of information about its energy system. It's just scattered around and hard to read.

We pull it together so you can type in a postcode and actually see it.

What would you most like to know about your energy that you can't find out?
